title: Windows and the Message Loop
summary: A Windows program with a window does not ask "has a key been pressed?". Windows tells it, by putting **messages** in a queue that the program reads in a **message loop** and hands to a **window procedure**. This lesson explains window classes, messages, the loop, and the variant games use so they can keep rendering when no messages arrive.
markdown:
## Event-driven programs A console program runs top to bottom and asks for input when it wants it. A windowed program is the other way round: it sits waiting, and the operating system **sends it events**: a key was pressed, the mouse moved, the window was resized, the window needs repainting, the user clicked Close. Windows delivers these as **messages**. Each message is a small structure: ```cpp struct MSG { HWND hwnd; // which window it is for UINT message; // what happened: WM_KEYDOWN, WM_MOUSEMOVE, WM_PAINT, ... WPARAM wParam; // extra information, meaning depends on the message LPARAM lParam; // more extra information DWORD time; POINT pt; }; ``` Every thread that creates a window gets a **message queue**. Windows appends messages to it; the program takes them out one at a time. ```mermaid flowchart LR U["User presses a key"] --> W["Windows"] W -->|"WM_KEYDOWN"| Q["Thread's message queue"] Q -->|"GetMessage"| L["Message loop"] L -->|"DispatchMessage"| P["Window procedure
WndProc(hwnd, msg, wParam, lParam)"] ``` ## Window classes and the window procedure Before creating a window you register a **window class**: a template naming, among other things, the **window procedure**, the function Windows calls for every message to windows of that class. It is a callback (lesson 3.04): you give Windows a function pointer, and Windows calls it. ```cpp LRESULT CALLBACK WindowProc(HWND hwnd, UINT message, WPARAM wParam, LPARAM lParam) { switch (message) { case WM_KEYDOWN: if (wParam == VK_ESCAPE) DestroyWindow(hwnd); // Esc closes the window return 0; case WM_DESTROY: PostQuitMessage(0); // ask the message loop to end return 0; } return DefWindowProcW(hwnd, message, wParam, lParam); // default handling for everything else } ``` The `switch` handles the messages the program cares about. Everything else **must** go to `DefWindowProcW`, which implements the standard behaviour: moving the window when its title bar is dragged, resizing, the system menu, closing on Alt+F4. A window procedure that returns 0 for everything produces a window that cannot be moved or closed. ## The message loop ```cpp MSG msg{}; while (GetMessageW(&msg, nullptr, 0, 0) > 0) { TranslateMessage(&msg); // turns key presses into WM_CHAR messages for typed text DispatchMessageW(&msg); // calls the window procedure of msg.hwnd } ``` - `GetMessageW` takes the next message from the queue, **waiting** if it is empty. It returns 0 when it finds `WM_QUIT`, which `PostQuitMessage` puts in the queue, and -1 on error. - `DispatchMessageW` looks up the window's class and calls its window procedure. That is the whole skeleton of every classic Windows program: register a class, create a window, loop until `WM_QUIT`. The next lesson writes a complete one. Some messages skip the queue entirely: Windows calls the window procedure **directly** for them (they are "sent" rather than "posted"), for example `WM_CREATE` during `CreateWindowExW` and `WM_SIZE` during resizing. So a window procedure can be called from inside other API calls, not only from `DispatchMessageW`. ## Messages you will handle most | Message | Sent when | Useful data | |---|---|---| | `WM_CREATE` | The window is being created | | | `WM_DESTROY` | The window is being destroyed | Post `WM_QUIT` here | | `WM_CLOSE` | The user asked to close (X button, Alt+F4) | Ask "save first?" here, or call `DestroyWindow` | | `WM_PAINT` | Part of the window needs redrawing | Use `BeginPaint` / `EndPaint` | | `WM_SIZE` | The client area changed size | New width and height in `lParam` | | `WM_KEYDOWN`, `WM_KEYUP` | A key went down or up | Virtual-key code in `wParam` (lesson 5.07) | | `WM_CHAR` | Text was typed (after `TranslateMessage`) | The UTF-16 character in `wParam` | | `WM_MOUSEMOVE`, `WM_LBUTTONDOWN`, ... | Mouse movement and buttons | Coordinates in `lParam` (lesson 5.07) | | `WM_TIMER` | A timer set with `SetTimer` fired | Timer id in `wParam` | | `WM_ACTIVATE` | The window gained or lost focus | Pause the game when it loses focus | ## The game loop variant `GetMessageW` waits when there are no messages. A game cannot wait: it must update and draw 60 or more times a second whether or not the player touches anything. Games use `PeekMessageW`, which returns immediately, and run a frame whenever the queue is empty: ```cpp bool running{ true }; while (running) { MSG msg{}; while (PeekMessageW(&msg, nullptr, 0, 0, PM_REMOVE)) // handle everything waiting... { if (msg.message == WM_QUIT) running = false; TranslateMessage(&msg); DispatchMessageW(&msg); } if (!running) break; updateGame(); // ...then run one frame renderGame(); } ``` Draining **all** waiting messages each frame, not just one, keeps input responsive and the window behaving normally. Chapter 10 builds the full game loop with proper timing around this. ## Common mistakes > [!warning] Not calling `DefWindowProcW` for unhandled messages > The window cannot be moved, resized or closed normally. > [!warning] Forgetting `PostQuitMessage` in `WM_DESTROY` > The window disappears but the message loop keeps waiting, and the process keeps running invisibly. Check Task Manager. > [!warning] Long work inside the window procedure > While it runs, no other messages are handled, and after a few seconds Windows marks the window "Not Responding". Do slow work elsewhere, or in steps. > [!warning] Using `GetMessageW` in a game > The game only updates when a message arrives, such as when the mouse moves. Use `PeekMessageW`. ## Knowledge check ```quiz ? What does `DispatchMessageW` do? + Calls the window procedure of the window the message is for - Puts a message in the queue - Translates key presses into characters > It finds the window's class and calls the function registered for it. ? A program's window closes but the process keeps running. What is the most likely cause? + `WM_DESTROY` does not call `PostQuitMessage`, so the message loop never ends - `DefWindowProcW` was called - The window class was not registered > The loop keeps waiting for messages for a window that no longer exists. ? Why do games use `PeekMessageW` instead of `GetMessageW`? + `PeekMessageW` returns immediately when the queue is empty, so the game can run a frame instead of waiting - `PeekMessageW` is faster at reading messages - `GetMessageW` does not work with games > A game must update continuously, not only when messages arrive. ? What should a window procedure do with a message it does not handle? + Pass it to `DefWindowProcW` and return its result - Return 0 - Ignore it and return 1 > The default procedure implements the standard window behaviour. ```
ideas:
- Read Microsoft's documentation for `WM_CLOSE` and work out what happens if the window procedure handles it and returns 0 without calling `DestroyWindow`.
- In the next lesson's program, add a `WM_ACTIVATE` case that prints whether the window gained or lost focus.
- Count how many messages per second a window receives while you move the mouse over it.

cards.a: The callback function, registered with the window class, that Windows calls with every message for windows of that class.

cards.q: How does a message loop end?
cards.a: `PostQuitMessage` puts `WM_QUIT` in the queue; `GetMessageW` returns 0 when it reads it, ending the loop.

cards.q: How does a game's loop differ from a classic message loop?
cards.a: It uses `PeekMessageW` to handle every waiting message without blocking, then runs one frame of update and rendering, and repeats.
